Title: Diagnosis

Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details:
- What the test asserts: testTooLargeFirstStep integrates a very short interval [0.0, 0.001] and asserts that every call to computeDerivatives(t, …) occurs with t within [start, end] (allowing only for nextAfter rounding).
- How the integrator initializes the first step:
  - DormandPrince853Integrator extends an embedded Runge–Kutta (ERK) integrator and delegates to AdaptiveStepsizeIntegrator.initializeStep(...) to compute the initial step size h.
  - In AdaptiveStepsizeIntegrator.initializeStep(...), h is computed from norms of y and y′ (lines 255–293). It is then clipped only against the configured minStep and maxStep (lines 295–300). Crucially, there is no check that |h| ≤ |tEnd − t0|.
- Where the overshoot happens:
  - In EmbeddedRungeKuttaIntegrator.integrate(...), the first step size hNew is computed via initializeStep(...) (lines 233–246) and is used immediately: stepSize = hNew (line 249).
  - Then the method evaluates intermediate stages: computeDerivatives(stepStart + c[k−1] * stepSize, …) (lines 252–263).
  - At this point, because initializeStep does not limit hNew to the remaining range, stepStart + c[k−1] * stepSize can exceed the user-specified end time t for very short ranges. This directly violates the test’s assertion that t ≤ end.
- Why later safeguards don’t help:
  - The code contains logic to keep the “next” step within the target after a step is accepted (lines 304–316), using filterStep(...) and clamping to t − stepStart if the next step would end beyond t.
  - However, there is no analogous filtering applied to the very first hNew right after initializeStep and before the first evaluation of derivatives. Thus, the function is evaluated out of the [start, end] interval even before any acceptance/rejection logic can correct it.
- Test-specific setup that enables the failure:
  - The test sets minStep = 0 and maxStep = 1.0 via setStepSizeControl(...) (lines 153–166). initializeStep(...) can therefore choose a large h (up to 1.0), unconstrained by the tiny integration range of 0.001. This large h results in computeDerivatives being called with times beyond end.

Conclusion: The initial step size for embedded Runge–Kutta integrators is not constrained by the remaining integration range before the first derivative evaluations. As a result, on very short intervals, the integrator evaluates the ODE at times beyond the requested end time, causing the test to fail. The fix is to apply the same “don’t overshoot the target” filtering to the very first step (immediately after initializeStep returns), just like what is already done for subsequent steps.
